slides.title: A model that doubles
slides.stem: If adoption keeps doubling every two years, what model could we use?

walk.cap: Let $E(t)$ be the percentage: start at $5$, double every $2$ years

graph.heading: A region adopts smartphones: $5\%$ of residents at $t=0$ and $10\%$ at $t=2$. Time $t$ is in years.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Four years on
slides.stem: Predict: what does the model give after four years?

walk.cap: Two more years doubles it again
walk.note: Adding $5$ again would give $15\%$. Doubling gives $20\%$.

graph.heading: A region adopts smartphones: $5\%$ of residents at $t=0$ and $10\%$ at $t=2$. Time $t$ is in years.

slides.title: Six years and eight years
slides.stem: Follow the model forward. What does it predict after six years? After eight years?

slides.title: Ten years on

slides.stem: As more residents adopt, what happens to the number still available to adopt? Describe in words how adoption should continue.

slides.title: Must it reach 100%?
slides.stem: Must the eventual level of adoption be $100\%$?

blocks.text: Some residents may never adopt due to cost, access, preference.

walk.note: Suppose adoption levels off at $80\%$. There is no equation yet, only the behaviour we need: early growth, then slowing towards a ceiling.

slides.title: Two proposals for the region
slides.stem: The region is considering two different actions. Read both carefully before matching them to a change in the model.

walk.note: The government pays part of the price of every phone. Residents who would have waited buy sooner, and some who could never afford one can now buy.
Smartphones reach the region earlier, so adoption has been under way for longer. At $t=0$, more residents already own a phone than the $5\%$ in our story.

slides.eyebrow: Beyond the story · Logistic growth around us
slides.title: Where else does it happen?

items.title: Yeast in sugar water
items.what: The number of yeast cells in a closed bottle of warm sugar water.
items.why: Cells divide quickly while there is plenty of sugar. Then the sugar runs low and waste builds up, so the population levels off at what the bottle can support.
items.exp: Put warm sugar water and a pinch of yeast in a clear bottle. Every 15 minutes for three hours, measure the height of the foam with a ruler. Foam height tracks how many cells are working. Plot height against time.

items.title: Duckweed on a tray of water
items.what: The number of duckweed fronds floating on a tray of pond water.
items.why: Every frond makes new fronds. As the surface fills, they crowd and shade each other, so growth slows towards the number the tray can hold.
items.exp: Start with 5 fronds in a tray by a window. Each day, photograph the tray from above and count the fronds. Keep going for about three weeks, then plot the count against days.

items.title: Bean seedling height
items.what: The height of a bean plant, measured every day from planting.
items.why: A seedling grows slowly at first, fastest in the middle of its life, then slows as it nears the height its species can reach.
items.exp: Plant several beans in pots on a windowsill. At the same time each day, measure each stem with a ruler. Average the heights and plot the average against days for six weeks.

items.title: Fish in a stocked pond
items.what: The number of fish after a pond is stocked with a few.
items.why: With food and space to spare, numbers climb quickly. Crowding and a limited food supply then hold the population near what the pond can support.
items.exp: Use mark and recapture. Tag 20 fish and release them. Later, catch a second sample and use the fraction that are tagged to estimate the total. Repeat each month. Practise first on a bowl of beans.

items.title: Flu in a school
items.what: The total number of people who have caught flu since the first case.
items.why: Early on, each sick student meets many healthy ones. Later most people have already had it, so new cases fall away and the total levels off.
items.exp: Play it as a class game. One student holds a card. Each round, every card holder taps one random classmate, who takes a card too. Count card holders after each round and plot the count against rounds.

items.title: Streaming subscribers
items.what: The total number of paying subscribers to a new streaming service.
items.why: Word of mouth speeds growth at first. Eventually most people who would ever subscribe already have, so the total flattens.
items.exp: Companies publish subscriber totals each quarter. Collect eight to twelve quarters from the service's first years, plot subscribers against quarter, and find where the curve bends.

items.title: Electric cars on the road
items.what: The share of cars in a country that are electric.
items.why: A few early adopters go first. The share then climbs quickly as prices fall and chargers spread, and slows as the market fills.
items.exp: Once a month, tally 100 cars in the school car park and record how many are electric. Plot the percentage against months for a year.

items.title: A viral video's views
items.what: The total views of a new video, day by day.
items.why: Each viewer shares it, so views surge. After a while most people who would watch it already have, so new views dry up.
items.exp: Pick a video posted today. At the same time each day for two weeks, note its view count. Plot total views against days and find the day with the most new views.

items.title: A rumour in a class
items.what: The number of students who have heard a piece of news.
items.why: Each student who knows it tells friends, so the number who know grows faster and faster. Later, few students are left who have not heard it.
items.exp: Tell one student a harmless message in the morning. At each break, ask everyone who knows it to raise a hand and count. Plot the count against the time of day.
